lessons.title: Clutches and transmissions
lessons.html:
Getting engine power to the ground

The propulsion system, or powertrain, carries engine torque to the wheels or tracks. On a tractor it must deliver very high torque at low speed for tillage and reasonable speed for road transport, often while also driving the PTO.

Clutches

A dry single-plate clutch uses a friction disc clamped between the flywheel and a pressure plate by springs. Pressing the pedal releases the clamp through the release bearing. Many tractors have a dual clutch: one stage for the transmission and one for the live PTO, so the PTO keeps running when the tractor stops. Wet clutches run in oil and are common in powershift and power-shuttle transmissions; they are engaged hydraulically. Clutch problems include slip, drag, judder and noise from the release bearing.

Transmission types

TypeHow it worksTypical use
Synchromesh manualDriver selects gears; synchronisers match speedsSmaller and utility tractors
Power shuttleHydraulic clutch packs change forward and reverse without the pedalLoader work
Partial and full powershiftClutch packs change gears under loadMid and large tractors
Continuously variable (CVT)Hydrostatic and mechanical paths combined for stepless speedModern high-horsepower tractors
HydrostaticHydraulic pump drives hydraulic motorCompact tractors, combines

Gear sets are arranged in ranges, for example low, medium and high, each with several gears, giving many speeds. A creeper range gives very low speeds for transplanting or trenching.

Transmission oil

Many tractors use one universal tractor transmission oil for the gearbox, hydraulics and wet brakes. Using the wrong oil can cause brake chatter, clutch slip and seal damage. Always use the specification in the manual.

lessons.title: Final drives, axles, wheels and tracks
lessons.html:
From transmission to ground

Differential and final drives

The crown wheel and pinion turn the drive through 90 degrees and reduce speed. The differential lets the left and right wheels turn at different speeds when turning. A differential lock joins them for traction in slippery conditions; it must be disengaged before turning or the tractor will fight the steering and parts can be damaged. Final drives, often planetary gear sets in the wheel ends, give a last large speed reduction and torque increase.

Front-wheel drive

On mechanical front-wheel drive (MFWD) tractors, a drive shaft from the transmission powers the front axle, which has its own differential and planetary hubs. The front axle is geared to turn slightly faster than the rear, called lead, so it pulls the tractor through. Wrong tyre sizes or pressures can upset this ratio, causing tyre wear and driveline stress. Articulated 4WD tractors steer by bending in the middle.

Wheels, tyres and ballast

Tyre type and pressure affect traction, soil compaction and fuel use. Set pressures for the load and work from the tyre maker's tables. Ballast, either cast weights or liquid in the tyres, helps traction; too little causes wheel slip, too much compacts soil and wastes fuel. Adjustable rear track width lets the wheels match crop rows.

Tracks

Rubber-tracked tractors spread weight over a larger area, reducing compaction and improving traction in wet soils. They need correct track tension and alignment, and regular checks of idlers, rollers and drive lugs.

Steering

Most modern tractors have hydrostatic steering: the steering wheel turns a valve that sends oil to a steering cylinder. There is no mechanical link, so a hydraulic failure makes steering very heavy.

Safety

Block wheels and support the tractor on stands before removing wheels. Large tractor tyres are very heavy; use a tyre handler. Never inflate a damaged or split-rim tyre without a cage.

Key points

  • The powertrain carries torque from the engine through clutch, transmission, differential and final drives.
  • Transmissions range from synchromesh to powershift, CVT and hydrostatic.
  • Disengage the diff lock before turning.
  • Use the oil specification in the manual for shared transmission and hydraulic systems.
  • Correct tyre size, pressure and ballast protect the driveline and soil.
